content: The use of high-dose vitamin interventions began in the 1950s, initially targeting patients with schizophrenia. Pyridoxine, also known as vitamin B6, was first administered to children diagnosed with autism syndrome after some children demonstrated improvements in speech and language abilities when given large doses of the vitamin. Subsequent studies explored the combined effects of vitamin B6 and magnesium (Mg) on various characteristics of autism, including verbal and non-verbal communication, interpersonal skills, and physiological functions. Magnesium was specifically included to mitigate the undesirable side effects associated with high doses of vitamin B6. The objective of this research was to evaluate the efficacy of the combined vitamin B6 and magnesium treatment (B6-Mg) in addressing social, communication, and behavioral challenges in children and adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and Dissertation Abstracts International, covering studies published up to April 2005. Additional studies were identified through reference lists of relevant articles. Only studies that involved participants diagnosed with ASD, where participants were randomly assigned to treatment or control groups, and where outcomes were compared to placebo or non-treated groups, were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers assessed and extracted data from the studies that met the inclusion criteria. The 2005 update of this review incorporated a new trial (Kuriyama 2002), bringing the total number of included studies to three, with a combined sample size of 33 participants. One of the studies (Tolbert 1993), which employed a crossover design, did not provide sufficient data for analysis. Another crossover study (Findling 1997) found no significant differences between the treatment and placebo groups in measures of social interaction, communication, compulsivity, impulsivity, or hyperactivity following the B6 intervention. The most recent study (Kuriyama 2002) was inspired by findings from epilepsy research and focused on a subgroup of children with pervasive developmental disorders (PDDs) who exhibited clinical features resembling those of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. This small study, involving only eight participants, measured IQ and Social Quotient and reported a statistically significant improvement in IQ (mean difference of 5.2, 95% confidence interval [0.2 to 10.3]) in the treated group, based on change scores. The authors concluded that, due to the limited number of studies, the small sample sizes, and the methodological limitations of the included studies, no definitive recommendation can be made regarding the use of vitamin B6 and magnesium as a treatment for autism spectrum disorder.
